content_voiceover: This table organizes familial thrombocytopenias by platelet size, and then splits each size category into syndromic forms, meaning there are other clinical features besides low platelets, versus non syndromic forms, where thrombocytopenia is essentially isolated. For giant platelets, the syndromic entity is MYH9 related disease, which includes May Hegglin anomaly, Sebastian, Fechtner, and Epstein syndromes, while the non syndromic counterpart is biallelic Bernard Soulier syndrome or TUBB1 related thrombocytopenia. For large platelets, syndromic causes include Paris Trousseau thrombocytopenia syndrome and GATA1 related disease, while non syndromic causes include monoallelic Bernard Soulier syndrome, gray platelet syndrome, and Glanzmann thrombasthenia. When platelet size is normal, syndromic causes include thrombocytopenia with absent radii and amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia with radio ulnar synostosis, while non syndromic causes include congenital amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia and familial platelet disorder with predisposition to AML, involving genes like ANKRD26, CYCS, and ETV6. Finally, for small platelets, the classic syndromic entity is Wiskott Aldrich syndrome and X linked thrombocytopenia, which for boards is a very testable, high yield association.
keypoints: Organize familial thrombocytopenias by platelet size then syndromic versus non syndromic
Giant platelets: MYH9 related disease is the classic syndromic cause
Large platelets: Paris Trousseau and GATA1 related disease are syndromic
Normal size: thrombocytopenia absent radii and CAMT are key entities
Small platelets: Wiskott Aldrich syndrome is the classic syndromic cause
keypoint_voiceover: For boards, memorize this table using platelet size as your anchor. Giant platelets point to MYH9 related disease, large platelets point to Paris Trousseau or GATA1 related disease, normal size points to TAR and congenital amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia, and small platelets point to Wiskott Aldrich syndrome.
